title: Serving Runtime Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook (Release Notes + Runbooks)
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview:

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture summary, kernel scheduling guidance, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite overview, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and pointers for the team wiki. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers and SREs responsible for runtime performance, deployment, and incident response.

Sections: 1) Architecture summary 2) Kernel scheduling and placement 3) Profiling playbook 4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration 5) Release notes (last two releases) 6) Known issues and mitigations 7) Runtime runbooks (operational) 8) Team wiki & onboarding links

1) Runtime architecture (summary)

- Purpose: low-latency, high-throughput transformer inference across hosted, dedicated and private deployments.
- Primary components:
  - Frontend gateway: HTTP/GRPC ingress, auth, routing, rate limits.
  - Smart router: policy-based routing (latency/cost/region/customer-tier).
  - Serving workers: GPU-backed containers running the inference engine.
  - KV cache: distributed cache (per-model prefix caching) for long-lived sessions.
  - Autoscaler: adjusts pool sizes based on queue depth and SLO targets.
  - Telemetry pipeline: traces, metrics (Prometheus), and token-level cost logs.

- Flow (high-level):
  1. Request arrives at gateway and is authenticated.
  2. Router selects model variant and target worker pool; applies fallback policies.
  3. Request either hits prefix cache or enters batching queue.
  4. Batch planned and dispatched to kernel execution on GPU via runtime.
  5. KV updates persisted and response streamed back.

- SLOs (target):
  | Metric | Target |
  |-------|--------|
  | P95 latency (text-gen, short prompts) | < 120ms |
  | P99 latency (text-gen) | < 250ms |
  | Availability (regional) | >= 99.95% |
  | Throughput (tokens/sec per GPU) | documented per model in model-catalog |

- Ownership: runtime-core owns pipelines and workers; eng-sre owns telemetry and alerting.

2) Kernel scheduling and placement

Principles:
- Maximize GPU utilization while meeting latency SLOs.
- Prefer smaller, latency-sensitive batches for premium-tier customers.
- Allow aggressive batching for cheap tiers during non-peak windows.

Scheduling layers:
- Local scheduler (worker-level): maintains CUDA stream pool, packs requests into contiguous tensors for a single kernel invocation, manages KV cache access. Key knobs: max_batch_size, batch_timeout_ms, preferred_sequence_alignment, quant_mode.
- Cluster scheduler (control plane): assigns requests to workers based on queue depth, data locality (KV hotness), and model compatibility. Implements capacity-aware routing and backpressure.

Config table (recommended defaults):
  - max_batch_size: 32
  - batch_timeout_ms: 12
  - preferred_sequence_alignment: 8
  - kv_prefetch: true
  - quant_mode: dynamic (fp16 with int8 fallback for supported kernels)

Tuning guidance (step-by-step):
1. Start from defaults above for a model family.
2. Run the benchmark suite with synthetic prompt distribution mirroring production (see section 4).
3. If P95 latency > target: reduce batch_timeout_ms by 2-5ms and re-run.
4. If GPU utilization < desired and latency headroom exists: increase max_batch_size in +8 increments.
5. For long sequences (>1024 tokens): consider sequence chunking and KV affinity to reduce recompute.
6. For private deployments with slower NVLink: prefer placement that reduces cross-socket transfers (use node-local pools).

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile an issue)

Goal: narrow root cause to kernel-level execution, memory pressure, or scheduling/backpressure. Follow the ordered checklist below.

Preconditions: profiling tools installed (nsys, nvprof legacy, CUPTI enabled builds, runtime metrics exporter). Ensure debug-level logging for the worker.

Step-by-step: 
1. Reproduce: capture the offending request(s) with request-id and timestamp.
2. Lightweight tracing: enable a 60s sampling window of runtime traces (trace-level=info) and collect Prometheus metrics (GPU utilization, memory, queue depth, batch sizes).
3. Kernel traces: run nsys capture for the worker during a focused test (3-10s) using the failing prompt set. Command example: 
``n
nsys profile --output profile_run1.nsys --capture-range=timerange --capture-range-start=0 --capture-range-end=10 --trace=cuda,osrt -- python3 run_load_test.py --prompts prompts/failure-set.json
``n
4. Analyze: open the nsys report and inspect kernel timelines, stream contention, and memcpy patterns. Key signals: long memcpy blocking kernels, serialized execution across streams, and extended kernel durations vs baseline.
5. Memory checks: look for OOM logs, allocator retries, and fragmentation; check per-GPU memory high watermark.
6. Scheduler logs: correlate batch packing decisions and queue reorderings. Look for excessive small batches or high batch abort rates.
7. Mitigation plan: based on findings, apply targeted changes (reduce batch_timeout_ms, adjust preferred_sequence_alignment, pin hot KV to local memory) and re-run profiling.

Common troubleshooting snippets:
- Dump last 500 scheduler decisions:
``n
curl -sS http://localhost:9101/debug/scheduler/last_decisions | jq '.' | tail -n 500
``n
- Collect Prometheus metrics for request-id ABC123:
``n
curl -sS 'http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=runtime_request_latency_ms%7Brequest_id%3D%22ABC123%22%7D'
``n
4) Benchmarking suite and CI integration

Overview: the benchmarking harness (bench/) contains workload definitions, prompt sets, and orchestration scripts for running performance regressions on CI or on dedicated benchmarking clusters.

Components:
- bench/bench-runner: runner that orchestrates load generation (locust-based), telemetry collection, and result packaging.
- bench/prompts/: curated prompt sets (short, medium, long, chat-session traces) with production-weighted distributions.
- bench/metrics-collector: post-processor that computes P50/P95/P99 latencies, tokens/sec, and cost-per-token estimates.

How to run locally (example):
1. Checkout repository and set environment variables: 
``n
export BENCH_TARGET=grpc://worker:50051
export PROMPTS=bench/prompts/short.json
./bench/bench-runner --model redwood-small --duration 300
``n
2. To run full suite on benchmark cluster: use the orchestration job in infra-ci: bench/full-suite.yaml (refer to infra repo CI pipeline).

CI gating: performance PRs must include bench run artifacts for affected models. The CI job fails the PR if P95 regresses by >7% compared to the stable baseline.

Interpreting results: 
- Primary signals: P95 latency, P99 latency, tokens/sec per-GPU, and cold-start penalty.
- Secondary signals: batch size distribution, queue depth, and KV hit-rate.

5) Release notes (recent important items)

Release 2026-02-20 (runtime v3.8.0) -- published
- Kernel selection logic improved: dynamic kernel selector now prefers fused attention kernels for seq_len <= 512, reducing P95 by 12% on Ampere GPUs.
- Added new KPI exporter labels token_cost and model_variant.
- Default batch_timeout_ms reduced from 15ms -> 12ms after lab experiments.
- Fixed a race in KV prefetch that could cause double fetch under heavy concurrency.

Release 2025-12-10 (runtime v3.7.1) -- published
- Introduced sequence alignment optimization that reduces padding wastage for mixed-length batches.
- Hotfix for memory leak in quantized int8 fallback path.

Upgrade guidance:
- Blue/green rollout recommended for clusters serving production traffic.
- Start with 10% canary, monitor P95 and error rate for 30 minutes, then ramp to 50% for 1 hour before full rollout.

6) Known issues and mitigations (current)

- Issue: occasional P99 spikes during autoscaler scale-up when many cold workers come up simultaneously.
  - Mitigation: stagger worker warmup by jittering startup by 5-20s and pre-warm KV caches when feasible.
- Issue: small-batch serialization on older drivers causing throughput loss.
  - Mitigation: pin to driver >= 525.x where available; enable stream-level parallelism flag as temporary workaround.
- Issue: on-prem NVLink topologies may cause cross-socket memcpy overhead for sequence lengths > 2048.
  - Mitigation: recommend node-local pools and affinity scheduling.

If you encounter an unknown issue, follow the runbook in section 7 and file a postmortem if outage > 15 minutes or customer impact is high.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)

A. Incident: Severe latency regression (P95 > target by 30% across region)
1. Triage (5 min): verify alert in PagerDuty, grab dashboards (per-route P95, batch-size histogram, queue depth).
2. Isolate (10 min): identify if regression is model-specific, pool-wide, or region-wide. Use query: service=\"runtime\" AND region=\"us-west\" AND model_variant.
3. Immediate mitigations (10-30 min):
  - Switch routing to lower-latency model variant or smaller-batch pool.
  - Temporarily increase worker pool size (scale-up) to reduce queuing.
  - If autoscaler stuck, perform manual scale or restart controller pod.
4. Deep-dive (post-stabilize): run profiling playbook to find root cause.
5. Postmortem: fill template (incident postmortem template in team wiki) within 72 hours.

B. Routine maintenance: kernel driver upgrades
1. Validate driver in staging with full bench suite.
2. Schedule blue/green rollout per cluster, apply driver, and validate P95 and memory footprints.

C. Runbook commands (quick)
- Restart scheduler: kubectl -n runtime rollout restart deployment/scheduler
- Collect nsys profile (see profiling playbook)
- Retrieve last 1k errors: kubectl logs deployment/worker -n runtime --tail=1000 | grep ERROR
